title: 10 Best Networking Books: What's Actually Worth Reading in 2026
summary: From Carnegie in 1936 to Sandstrom's 2026 research on talking to strangers. Ten books, what each one is good at, and who should skip it.
body_markdown:
Most networking book lists have the same problem. They name ten titles, call each one essential, and never tell you what any of them are for. You end up buying three and finishing none.


This list is sorted by publication year, from 1936 to this spring, because the arc matters. The early books are about charm and first impressions. The recent ones are about research: who actually passes you useful information, what a conversation is really doing, what happens when you talk to a stranger on a train. The field got a lot more empirical, and the newer books are better for it.


Every entry below says what the book is good at and who should skip it.


**Fast facts:**


-


Six titles from the previous version of this list were cut, including two by the same author and one that was really a public-speaking book.


-


The oldest entry is from 1936 and still outsells most of the others.


-


Four of the ten are written by or for introverts.


-


The newest, Gillian Sandstrom's[Once Upon a Stranger](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0063385414) , came out in March 2026 and is built on her own experiments.

## 1. How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936)


**Dale Carnegie.**[How to Win Friends and Influence People on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0671027034)


Ninety years on, this is still the book everyone means when they say "that networking book." Carnegie breaks social interaction into principles with names like "become genuinely interested in other people" and illustrates each with a story about a salesman or a president.


The advice holds up better than it has any right to, mostly because it's about attention. Carnegie's core move is to stop performing and start listening, which is still the thing most people get wrong.


The criticism is fair, though. It's anecdote all the way down, with no research behind it, and the framing of relationships as things to be won and influenced reads as manipulative to a modern ear. Read it for the fundamentals and take the persuasion chapters lightly.


**Skip it if:** you want evidence rather than storytelling. Grant and Burkus do the same territory with data.


## 2. Never Eat Alone (2005, expanded 2014)


**Keith Ferrazzi with Tahl Raz.**[Never Eat Alone on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0385346654)


Ferrazzi's book is the operations manual of networking. Where Carnegie is about how to be in a conversation, Ferrazzi is about the system around it: who you keep track of, when you reach out, how you turn a meal into a relationship.


The useful part is his insistence that you contact people before you need anything. His "ping" concept, a short no-agenda message just to stay present, is the single most transferable idea in the book, and it's what most people fail to do.


The tone is a lot. Ferrazzi is a relentless, wildly extroverted networker and the book reads that way. If you find that exhausting, take the mechanics and leave the persona.


**Skip it if:** hustle culture makes your skin crawl. Wickre's book covers similar ground for people who'd rather not.


## 3. The Charisma Myth (2012)


**Olivia Fox Cabane.**[The Charisma Myth on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1591845947)


Cabane's argument is that charisma is a set of learnable behaviors rather than something you're born with, which is genuinely encouraging if you've always assumed you lack it. She breaks it into presence, power, and warmth, and defines four charisma styles so you can work with your own temperament instead of against it.


The practical exercises are the strength here. There's real, specific guidance on eye contact, pausing, and managing your own discomfort before a conversation starts.


It's not a networking book, and the psychological research it leans on is thinner than the confident tone suggests. Treat the mechanics as useful and the science as loose.


**Skip it if:** you want tactics for building a network rather than for being in a room.


## 4. The Startup of You (2012, revised 2022)


**Reid Hoffman and Ben Casnocha.**[The Startup of You on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0307888908)


Written by LinkedIn's co-founder, this one treats your career like a company: you have a competitive position, you take calculated risks, and your network is the asset that makes both possible. The 2022 revision updates the examples, which the original badly needed.


The section on what Hoffman calls "network intelligence" is the part worth the price. It reframes your contacts as a source of information rather than a source of favors, which changes how you use them.


The startup framing gets strained in places, and the perspective is unmistakably Silicon Valley. If you work in a field where careers move slowly and relationships are built over decades, some of it won't land.


**Skip it if:** you're not in or adjacent to tech.


## 5. Give and Take (2013)


**Adam Grant.**[Give and Take on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0143124986)


Grant sorts people into givers, takers, and matchers, then shows that givers cluster at both the bottom and the top of success distributions. The difference between the two groups is the interesting part: successful givers set limits, and unsuccessful ones don't.


This is the most rigorous book on the list. Grant is an organizational psychologist and the claims come with studies attached.


The writing is dense and the case studies run long. Several readers find the middle third heavy going.


**Skip it if:** you already know generosity is your default and your actual problem is saying no. Grant diagnoses that but doesn't spend much time fixing it.

## 6. Friend of a Friend (2018)


**David Burkus.**[Friend of a Friend on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0544971264)


Burkus makes the case that the network you need already exists and you're just not seeing it properly. Rather than telling you to meet more people, he walks through the social science of how networks are structured: weak ties, dormant ties, structural holes, clusters.


The chapter on dormant ties is the one people remember. Contacts you haven't spoken to in years are often the most useful people you can call, because they've spent those years somewhere you haven't. They're also far easier to reach out to than strangers, since the relationship already exists.


If you want a script for what to say at a conference, this isn't it. Burkus explains how networks behave and leaves the execution to you.


**Skip it if:** you want step-by-step instructions rather than a mental model. It pairs well with our[strength of weak ties](https://getdex.com/blog/strength-of-weak-ties/) explainer.


## 7. Taking the Work Out of Networking (2018)


**Karen Wickre.**[Taking the Work Out of Networking on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1501199285)


Wickre spent years at Google and Twitter and describes herself as an introvert who never worked a room in her life. Her method is what she calls loose-touch habits: small, low-effort, repeated contact instead of intense bursts of event networking.


The book is at its best on the specifics of staying in touch without a reason. Forwarding an article, a two-line congratulations note, a check-in after a job change. None of it requires performing, which is exactly why it works for the people other networking books fail.


The advice is deliberately modest in scope. If you're already comfortable at conferences and want to scale up, this won't add much.


**Skip it if:** you enjoy events and your problem is volume rather than dread.


## 8. Digital Body Language (2021)


**Erica Dhawan.**[Digital Body Language on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1250246520)


This fills a gap none of the older books touch: most professional relationships now run through text. Slack, email, and video calls strip out tone, facial expression, and timing, and Dhawan's argument is that we've replaced those cues with new ones we never agreed on.


Some of it sounds trivial until you think about it. Response time reads as respect. A period at the end of a one-word reply reads as anger to some people and as nothing at all to others. Whether you turn your camera on is a signal whether you meant it to be or not.


Parts of it are already dated, and the generational-difference sections lean on broad claims. The core observation is sound anyway.


**Skip it if:** your working relationships are mostly built in person.


## 9. Supercommunicators (2024)


**Charles Duhigg.**[Supercommunicators on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0593243919)


Duhigg's framework is that every conversation is one of three types, and most failures come from two people having different ones at the same time. There's the practical conversation (what's this about?), the emotional one (how do we feel?), and the social one (who are we?). Matching the type your counterpart is in is the skill.


The reporting is excellent, as you'd expect from Duhigg. A jury room, a CIA recruitment, an oncologist and a patient. The case studies carry the theory.


It's about conversation rather than networking, so there's nothing here about tracking contacts or building a network over time. Useful anyway, since the conversations that make a relationship stick are usually the hard ones.


**Skip it if:** you specifically want networking strategy.


## 10. Once Upon a Stranger (2026)


**Gillian Sandstrom.**[Once Upon a Stranger on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0063385414)


Published in March 2026, this is the newest thing on the list and the only one written by the researcher whose own experiments it describes. Sandstrom is a psychologist who studies what she calls minimal social interactions, the brief exchanges with baristas, commuters, and dog walkers that most people assume don't count.


Her finding is that they count more than we expect, and that we're consistently wrong about how they'll go. People predict that talking to a stranger will be awkward and unwelcome, then report enjoying it. She's also an introvert, and the book takes the anxiety seriously instead of telling you to push through it.


It's about connection generally rather than professional networking, so don't expect career tactics. But if the hard part for you is starting, this is the most useful book here.


**Skip it if:** small talk already comes easily and your problem is what happens after.


## What none of these books solve


Read all ten and you'll know exactly what to do. Whether you then do it every week for a year is a separate question, and it's the one that decides whether any of this was worth the reading time.


Because every book here lands on the same instruction eventually: stay in touch before you need something. Ferrazzi calls it pinging, Wickre calls it loose touch, Burkus points at dormant ties. They agree, and almost nobody follows through, because nothing in an ordinary week prompts you to.


The software most people already have doesn't help. A calendar only knows about meetings someone has already booked, and an inbox only knows about people who already wrote to you. The contact going quietly cold shows up in neither, which is precisely the problem.

-


If your problem is that you know plenty of people and never follow up, no book will fix that. A[system](https://getdex.com/docs/workflows/keep-in-touch) will.


-


If you're deep in a specialist field where your reputation is your work, reading about rapport is a poor use of the hours. Publish instead.


-


If you've read two of these already, a third is procrastination. The overlap between them is substantial by design.


-


If networking as a concept makes you uncomfortable, Sandstrom and Wickre take that seriously. The other eight mostly don't.

## Frequently Asked Questions About the Best Networking Books of 2026


### What is the best networking book for beginners?


[Never Eat Alone](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0385346654) by Keith Ferrazzi is the usual starting point because it covers the full system: who to track, when to reach out, and how to follow up. If Ferrazzi's high-energy style doesn't suit you, Karen Wickre's[Taking the Work Out of Networking](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1501199285) covers the same ground for people who dislike events.


### What is the best networking book for introverts?


Karen Wickre's[Taking the Work Out of Networking](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1501199285) (2018) and Gillian Sandstrom's[Once Upon a Stranger](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0063385414) (2026) are both written by self-described introverts. Wickre focuses on low-effort ongoing contact; Sandstrom focuses on the anxiety of starting a conversation and the research showing it goes better than people expect.


### Is How to Win Friends and Influence People still worth reading in 2026?


Yes, with caveats. Carnegie's core advice about paying genuine attention to other people has held up since 1936. The book has no research behind it and its persuasion framing can read as manipulative, so it works best as a foundation rather than a complete guide.


### Do networking books actually work?


They're good at changing how you think about relationships and poor at changing what you do week to week. The recurring instruction across every book on this list is to stay in touch before you need something, which is a habit problem rather than a knowledge problem. Most people need a reminder system, not more reading.


### What is a personal CRM, and do I need one?


A personal CRM is software for tracking personal and professional relationships, like a sales CRM but built for an individual. Tools such as Dex import contacts from LinkedIn, Gmail, and WhatsApp, then track notes, job changes, and reminders for when to reach back out. If you already remember everyone in your network, you don't need one.


### Which networking book has the best research behind it?


Adam Grant's[Give and Take](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0143124986) and David Burkus's[Friend of a Friend](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0544971264) are the most rigorously sourced, both drawing on published organizational and social psychology. Gillian Sandstrom's[Once Upon a Stranger](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0063385414) is unusual in that the author ran the studies she writes about.
